lead: Above a safe cabin altitude the air holds too little oxygen for the body. The oxygen system raises the partial pressure of oxygen in the lungs by supplying stored gas, liquid oxygen, a chemical generator or, mostly in military aircraft, on-board generation. It protects the crew in a decompression and gives passengers time while the aircraft descends. Oxygen also makes oil and grease burn fiercely, so the system has its own safety rules.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.6 for cabin altitude and Chapter 2.2 for bleed air.

sections.h3: Hypoxia and the need for oxygen

blocks.text: Hypoxia is a shortage of oxygen reaching the body tissues. It starts with headache and poor judgement, then leads to loss of consciousness. In an aircraft it is caused by low outside pressure: the fraction of oxygen in air stays near 0.21, but the total pressure falls, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls with it.

blocks.where: P<sub>O2</sub> is the partial pressure of oxygen in bar; F<sub>O2</sub> is the oxygen fraction (0.21 in air); P<sub>amb</sub> is ambient pressure in bar. At sea level P<sub>amb</sub> ≈ 1.013 bar gives P<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.213 bar. At 35,000 ft P<sub>amb</sub> ≈ 0.24 bar gives P<sub>O2</sub> ≈ 0.050 bar.

blocks.text: Cabin pressurisation keeps the cabin at a safe pressure altitude, often 6000 to 8000 ft. If pressurisation fails, the crew needs supplemental oxygen at once. The time of useful consciousness (TUC) is the time from losing oxygen to being unable to act usefully. Standard tables give about 3 to 5 minutes at 25 000 ft, 30 to 60 s at 35 000 ft and 15 to 20 s at 40 000 ft, so crew masks must be on within seconds.

Supplemental oxygen raises F<sub>O2</sub> in the mask above 0.21, up to pure oxygen at high cabin altitude, so P<sub>O2</sub> in the lungs stays near its sea-level value while P<sub>amb</sub> is low. It buys the time needed to descend.

Four supply types are common. High-pressure gaseous oxygen sits in cylinders at about 1,800 psi (124 bar). A filler valve fills the cylinder; a shut-off valve isolates it; a regulator reduces pressure; a mask delivers gas to the user. Liquid oxygen (LOX) stores more oxygen in less volume, but it must be kept cold and it boils off; it is used where weight and space matter. A chemical oxygen generator burns a sodium chlorate candle to release oxygen; it is simple and needs no pressure storage, but once started it cannot be stopped. Military aircraft often use an on-board oxygen generating system (OBOGS), which separates oxygen from engine bleed air with a molecular sieve.

Crew masks use a regulator. A demand regulator opens only when the user inhales. A diluter-demand regulator mixes cabin air with oxygen at low cabin altitude and goes to pure oxygen as cabin altitude rises. A pressure-demand regulator supplies oxygen slightly above cabin pressure so the mask stays sealed and the lungs get oxygen at very high cabin altitude or in smoke. Passenger masks are continuous-flow: a simple pressure reducer, or the chemical generator itself, feeds a fixed flow to each mask whether or not the passenger is breathing in. Most airliners supply passengers from chemical generators that run for roughly 12 to 22 minutes, long enough for an emergency descent.

Other parts are tubing, a pressure gauge, a relief valve and an overboard discharge disc that bursts if the cylinder is overpressured. The gauge reads cylinder pressure, not the mass of gas left. By Boyle’s law at constant temperature, the gas available at 1 bar is V₁ = V<sub>w</sub> × (P<sub>c</sub> − P<sub>r</sub>) ÷ P₁, where V<sub>w</sub> is the cylinder water volume in L, P<sub>c</sub> the cylinder pressure in bar, P<sub>r</sub> the reserve pressure that is not used, and P₁ = 1 bar.

Before flight the crew checks cylinder pressure and the mask seal. The crew dons masks when cabin altitude passes about 10 000 ft (the cabin altitude warning), and selects 100 % or emergency pressure for smoke. If cabin altitude passes about 14 000 ft, the passenger panels open automatically and the masks drop out; this automatic release is called mask drop-out. The passenger then pulls the mask down, which pulls a pin and starts the flow. Portable cylinders serve walk-around use.

items: Check cylinder pressure and the mask seal before flight.
Open the shut-off valve slowly and set the regulator to normal.
Don the mask at the cabin altitude warning, about 10 000 ft.
Above about 14 000 ft passenger masks drop out automatically; the passenger pulls one down to start the flow.

blocks.text: Oxygen is not fuel, but it makes fuel and oil burn fiercely. Fittings must be cleaned for oxygen service; no grease, oil or PTFE tape on threads. Open cylinder valves slowly to avoid a pressure surge and adiabatic heating. Keep cylinders away from heat and secure them so they do not become missiles. A chemical generator becomes hot; do not cover it. A LOX converter vents oxygen; keep it away from ignition sources. In a fire, shut off supply if possible and use the fire procedure in Chapter 2.9.

spec.aria: An oxygen cylinder of 50 litres at 124 bar feeds a shut-off valve and a pressure reducer, then a low-pressure manifold with six mask symbols standing for twelve masks at 4 litres per minute each, 48 litres per minute in all. A box works the usable gas, 5700 litres, and the duration, 118.75 minutes.

examples.question: A passenger oxygen cylinder has a water volume of 50 L and is filled to 124 bar. It must be refilled when it falls to 10 bar, so gas below 10 bar is not counted. Twelve passengers each draw 4 L/min measured at 1 bar. Ignore temperature change. Find the usable gas, the total flow and how long the supply lasts.
steps: Usable gas at 1 bar: V₁ = V<sub>w</sub> × (P<sub>c</sub> − P<sub>r</sub>) ÷ P₁ = 50 × (124 − 10) ÷ 1 = 5700 L.
In hours: 118.75 ÷ 60 = 1.98 h, about 1 h 59 min.
examples.answer: The cylinder gives 5700 L of usable gas at 48 L/min, which lasts about 119 minutes.

traps: Reading cylinder pressure as quantity: the gas available is water volume × usable pressure, and the gauge pressure also changes with temperature even when no gas is used.
Using oil or grease on oxygen fittings: oxygen makes these burn fiercely, so oxygen service cleaning is mandatory.
Confusing diluter-demand with pressure-demand: a diluter-demand regulator mixes cabin air at low altitude; a pressure-demand regulator supplies oxygen above cabin pressure.
Assuming a chemical generator can be switched off: once the sodium chlorate candle starts, it supplies oxygen until it is finished.
Mixing up passenger and crew masks: passenger masks are continuous-flow and drop out automatically; crew masks use diluter-demand or pressure-demand regulators.

quiz.q: Define hypoxia and time of useful consciousness.
quiz.a: Hypoxia is a shortage of oxygen reaching body tissues. Time of useful consciousness is the time from oxygen loss to inability to act correctly.

quiz.q: Why does a diluter-demand regulator mix cabin air with oxygen at low cabin altitude?
quiz.a: At low cabin altitude the ambient partial pressure of oxygen is enough for the body. Mixing cabin air with oxygen saves stored oxygen and still gives the required partial pressure. As cabin altitude rises, the regulator increases the oxygen fraction and goes to pure oxygen.

quiz.q: A 40 L water-volume cylinder is at 150 bar and is used down to 10 bar. Ten passengers each use 5 L/min at 1 bar. Find the usable gas at 1 bar and the duration.
quiz.a: Usable gas = 40 × (150 − 10) ÷ 1 = 5600 L. Total flow = 10 × 5 = 50 L/min. Duration = 5600 ÷ 50 = 112 min.

quiz.q: Crew masks are pressure-demand, passenger masks are continuous-flow. Give one operational reason for each choice.
quiz.a: A pressure-demand crew mask keeps a positive seal and gives oxygen above cabin pressure during rapid decompression or smoke, when the crew must stay alert. A continuous-flow passenger mask is simple, cheap, needs no inhalation valve and lets many passengers share a supply; the crew assists those who cannot pull the mask.

quiz.q: What is a sodium chlorate candle?
quiz.a: A chemical oxygen generator. It burns a sodium chlorate mixture to release oxygen for masks, and once started it cannot be stopped.

quiz.q: Why must oxygen system fittings be free of grease and oil?
quiz.a: Oxygen makes grease and oil burn fiercely. A small amount of oil in a high-pressure oxygen fitting can ignite and cause a fire or explosion, so oxygen service cleaning is required.

quiz.q: A chemical oxygen generator has started. Can the crew stop the oxygen flow by closing a valve? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The candle produces oxygen by a chemical reaction and has no shut-off valve in the generator. The crew can only remove the mask or isolate the affected supply line if the installation provides one; the generator itself runs until the candle is finished.

quiz.q: At 35,000 ft the ambient pressure is 0.24 bar. Oxygen fraction is 0.21. Find P<sub>O2</sub> and compare with sea level, where P<sub>amb</sub> is 1.013 bar.
quiz.a: At 35 000 ft: P<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 0.24 = 0.050 bar. At sea level: P<sub>O2</sub> = 0.21 × 1.013 = 0.213 bar. The high-altitude value is about a quarter of the sea-level value (0.050 ÷ 0.213 = 0.24).

beyond: Not for the exam. Military OBOGS uses a zeolite molecular sieve to adsorb nitrogen from bleed air and leave oxygen-rich gas; the sieve beds alternate between production and purge. Newer civil designs use electronic pulse-demand portable oxygen to save gas for walk-around crew. Research looks at lighter composite cylinders and oxygen concentrators for long-endurance aircraft. Search next for OBOGS, molecular sieve oxygen concentrator and chemical oxygen generator maintenance.
